texto: The first note was taped to my door on a Tuesday
morning in February. It was written in blue
ink on the back of a grocery receipt, in careful, slanted handwriting. It said,
’Please stop pacing at three in the morning. I can
hear every step. Thank you. Ruth downstairs.’
I read it three times, standing in the hallway
with my keys in my hand. I wasn’t annoyed.
I was embarrassed. I was twenty-seven. I had been
living alone in that apartment for about
four months, and I really liked Ruth. She was
the older woman who lived in the downstairs
unit of our duplex, a retired school teacher
who always had her porch light on and her
television a little too loud. The last thing I wanted was to be the noisy neighbor.
The problem was that I didn’t pace. Not at three in the morning, not at any time.
I worked early shifts, doing admin at a hospital,
and I was usually asleep by ten. I sleep like
a rock. My sister used to say you could move
my bed across the room with me in it and I
didn’t notice.
The apartment itself was the upstairs half of
an old house in Columbus, Ohio. Hardwood
floors, radiators that clanked every time the
heat came on. One long hallway that ran
from the living room past the bathroom to my bedroom at the back.
There was a narrow coat closet in that hallway
that I never used. The landlord told me when
I moved in that there was a plumbing access panel
at the back of it, and that if anything
ever leaked, that was where the shutoff was.
I’d opened the closet once, saw a painted
square of plywood held in with screws, and closed it again.
That evening, I knocked on Ruth’s door to apologize anyway. She was sweet about it.
She said she hadn’t wanted to bother me, but
it had been going on for a few weeks and
she wasn’t sleeping well. I asked her what exactly
she was hearing. She thought about
it for a second and said, ’It’s slow. Back and forth. From your living room, down
the hallway, and back again. Like someone thinking
about something.’ She said it usually
started a little after three and went on for twenty minutes or so. Then it stopped,
and she heard a door close. I told her it couldn’t have been me. I told
her about the early shifts and how heavy a sleeper
I was. She gave me this kind, patient
look, the way you’d look at a student who swore they’d done their homework, and said
maybe I was sleepwalking. She said her late husband
used to do it, and he never believed
her either. I laughed it off, but it bothered me. When
I got back upstairs, I noticed little things
I’d been ignoring. The thermostat was set
to sixty-eight, and I always kept it at sixty-five
because the heat was expensive. There was
a grey hoodie I’d been looking for since Christmas, and I’d assumed I left it at
my sister’s. A container of leftover pasta I
was sure I hadn’t finished was gone from
the fridge. Every one of those things had an
easy explanation, and every one of them,
on its own, was nothing. I told myself I was being dramatic.
But I did something about the sleepwalking idea.
That night, before bed, I set my phone
on the little table by the couch and started a
voice recording, and I let it run all night.
In the morning, I almost didn’t listen to it.
Seven hours of a quiet apartment didn’t
seem worth the time. But on my lunch break,
I opened it and scrolled through the audio
waveform, looking for anything that wasn’t a
flat line. Most of it was just the hum of
the refrigerator and the radiator ticking. Then, at three-eleven in the morning, the
line started to move. I put my earbuds in and pressed play. At first,
it was just a creak, the long, low creak an old
floorboard makes when weight settles on
it slowly. Then another one, a little closer. Then
footsteps. Not the quick, careless steps
of someone walking to the bathroom. Slow ones.
Heel, then toe, like someone trying very hard
not to make noise. They crossed the living room
right past my phone, went down the hallway,
and stopped. I knew exactly where they stopped because
there’s one board outside my bedroom door that pops when you step on it, and I heard
it pop. Then nothing. For almost a full minute,
there was no sound on the recording at all.
And then, very faintly, I heard breathing, slow
and even, right outside my bedroom door,
while I was asleep on the other side of it. I
sat in my car in the hospital parking garage
and listened to that minute four times. Then
the steps went back up the hallway, slowly,
and I heard a soft click, like a door being pulled
shut. The only door in that hallway,
besides mine and the bathroom, was the coat closet.
I called my sister, and she told me to call
the police. I didn’t, and I know how that
sounds. I kept thinking about how I would go.
A woman calls and says she heard footsteps
on her own phone recording, in her own apartment,
where she lives alone. They tell me I was
sleepwalking, just like Ruth did. I wanted proof,
something no one could explain away.
So after work, I drove to an electronics store and bought a cheap Wi-Fi camera,
the kind people use to watch their dogs. I set it
on top of the bookshelf in the living room,
angled so I could see the couch, the kitchen doorway,
and the start of the hallway. I tested
it with my phone. The picture was grainy, but in
night mode, you could see everything in shades
of grey. Then I packed a bag and went to sleep
at my sister’s place. I told myself it was an
experiment. If the camera showed nothing, I’d go
home, admit I was sleepwalking, and buy Ruth
a fruit basket. My sister made up the couch for
me, and I lay there with my phone on my chest,
opening the app every half hour to look at my empty living room.
I must have fallen asleep around one. The notification woke me up. Motion detected,
living room, at 3.14 a.m. I opened the feed, and there was a man in my apartment.
He was standing in the middle of my living room,
barefoot, in the grey hoodie I’d been missing
since Christmas. He was thin, maybe in his forties,
with his hair grown out and pushed behind his
ears. He wasn’t searching for anything. He wasn’t
stealing anything. He was just walking,
very slowly, from the couch to the start of
the hallway and back again, with his hands
folded in front of him, exactly the way Ruth described
it, like someone thinking about something.
At one point, he stopped at the kitchen doorway and
stood there with his head tilted, listening.
Then he went into the kitchen, opened my refrigerator, and stood in the light of it,
eating something out of a container with his fingers. He put the container back,
he wiped his hand on the hoodie, and then he walked down the hallway,
opened the coat closet, stepped inside, and pulled the door shut behind him.
I woke my sister up, and this time I called 911. The
officers who met me there an hour later were
polite and, honestly, I think they expected to find
nothing. They checked every room, every window,
and under my bed. Then I pointed to the coat
closet, and one of them opened it with his
flashlight out. The square of plywood at the back
was still there, but the screws were gone.
It was only leaning in place. When he pulled
it away, there was a dark gap behind it,
about two feet high, that ran between the floors of
the house, above Ruth's ceiling, and under mine.
They didn't find him. There was a vent at the far
end of that crawlspace that opened onto the
side of the house, and its cover had been pried loose
from the inside. But they found where he'd
been living. A camping pad and a sleeping bag,
granola bar wrappers, and a lot of my food
containers, cleaned and stacked. A phone charger,
plugged into an outlet that, it turned out, was
on the back of my bedroom wall. And a spiral notebook.
One of the officers showed me a page
of that notebook, and I wish he hadn't. It was my schedule,
when I left for work, when I came home,
which nights I did laundry, what time my bedroom
light usually went off. On the last page,
in very small, neat handwriting, it said, she sleeps very deeply.
The detective who called me the next week said they
had a name, a man who'd been evicted from
a house two streets over the summer before. They believed
he'd been living in that crawlspace since
before I signed my lease, longer than I had lived there.
I broke my lease and moved in with my sister
for a while. Ruth cried when I told her what happened.
She kept saying she was sorry, that
she should have known it wasn't me, that she should

They never found him. I checked the news sometimes for his name. Nothing. Ruth still
sends me a card every Christmas. Last spring she
called me, just to catch up. She told me
the landlord had fixed up the apartment, and a new
girl had moved in upstairs, a nursing student.
She said the girl was sweet and very quiet. She just
wished she wouldn't pace so much at night.
